Summary

WAI’s early field-building

Wild Animal Initiative (WAI) launched in early 2019 with the objective of establishing a mainstream scientific field dedicated to the practical study of wild animal welfare (hereafter referred to as “wild animal welfare science” or WAWS). We chose to approach the problem of wild animal suffering through scientific field-building because there were (and remain) many critical questions requiring empirical research before we could know that any wild animal welfare intervention or policy is having a net-positive impact. The study of wild animal welfare requires concepts, methods and skills from both ecology and animal welfare science, but at the time, there were very few scientists studying the welfare of free-living wild animals and there was little crossover between these fields in terms of projects, conferences, or academic programs. Although it would be possible to hire scientists from one of these fields and cross-train them to do research outside of academia (as indeed we do at Wild Animal Initiative on our research team), academic institutions provide a number of efficiencies, such as access to specialized laboratory equipment, field sites, agreements with publishers, and a culture of peer review. By funding academic research, we could take advantage of expertise and infrastructure all over the world, which would also allow us to reach more animals. By helping to coordinate WAWS into a recognized academic field, we could multiply the impact of the research we fund by making its importance clearer to other scientists and decision-makers, and by potentially attracting mainstream funding from universities and agencies to support more WAWS projects.

Our first challenge was establishing awareness and legitimacy of WAWS as a useful, scientifically compelling and tractable area of research. This would attract scientists from adjacent fields to integrate WAWS concepts and methods into their current research, providing experience that would reveal to them and us their level of enthusiasm and aptitude for long-term engagement with the field.

In those first few years, we emphasized areas of overlap with the adjacent fields of ecology, conservation and captive animal welfare science. We asked researchers in these fields to give WAWS a try. For ecologists that meant trying to interpret physiology and behavior in terms of welfare or measuring putative welfare indicators alongside their population and habitat-scale metrics, while for captive animal welfare scientists that meant developing welfare indicators for species with large wild populations or devising new methods to make captive-based welfare assessment methods feasible to apply in the wild. The support of Coefficient Giving, beginning in 2021, allowed us to launch a grants program and enable many more ecologists and captive animal welfare scientists the opportunity to try their hand at wild animal welfare research. This supercharged our field-building work. Beyond the handful of projects we could actually afford to fund, the prospect of receiving a grant incentivized hundreds more researchers to submit proposals engaging with the concepts and methods we wrote about and collaboratively advised them on.

As we started to see repeat grantees and increasingly relevant projects being proposed, we shifted emphasis away from encouraging researchers to ‘try’ WAWS by simply integrating it with their existing research programs, and increasingly emphasized the challenging priority areas and concerns that make the field distinct and will be necessary to inform responsible wild animal welfare interventions. See for example the text of our 2023 call for Seed Grant (<$30k) proposals or our most recent (2025) call for proposals.

As someone who has been with Wild Animal Initiative since the beginning (coming from a PhD in molecular ecology and working part-time on academic outreach at Animal Ethics), if you told me back then that this would be the state of wild animal welfare science in 2026, I would be thrilled. Especially in the past year, we have begun to see important external signals of field-building milestones being reached, including:

  • WAI co-organized the 2025 meeting of the UK’s Animal Welfare Research Network, with approximately a third of the conference dedicated to wild animal welfare. We will be doing something similar for the Spanish-language equivalent, RedCIBA, this year, and have been invited to sponsor themed sessions at several other conferences. WAI’s staff researchers have organized workshops and sessions at many other conferences over the years; what is new here is the scale of our involvement and that we are being invited.
  • WAI’s research team was invited to curate a special issue of the highly regarded journal, Integrative & Comparative Biology, focused on wild animal welfare. This is a huge opportunity and a field-building milestone that they noticed WAI’s research and thought that wild animal welfare would be a compelling theme for their readership.
  • We are seeing more collaborations emerge organically among WAI grantees, and concrete interest in establishing WAWS academic institutions. Within the next six months, we expect to support the launch of the first academic center dedicated to the ecological dimension of wild animal welfare, spearheaded by a cluster of WAI grantees and benefiting from university co-funding. This will complement the NYU Wild Animal Welfare Program, which focuses more on policy analysis. Earlier this year, we also made a grant to Scotland’s Rural College (SRUC) to develop a standalone wild animal welfare module that would connect students from their animal welfare and conservation MSc programs, as well as create a wild animal welfare scholarship and fund small student research projects in wild animal welfare.

Our theory of change has always been centered on academic field-building, as we think that is the only way to get research done at scale with the credibility that will be required to bring positive policy attention to wild animal welfare (on that note, we’re excited to work with the new policy-focused CWAW!). The foundation of WAWS laid so far

Developing the science necessary to inform responsible wild animal welfare interventions that can meaningfully impact most animals is a huge, long-term endeavor, and most of that impact will be felt only after a sustainable, mission-aligned academic field is established. To that end, we have seen meaningful progress through our grants and internal research towards identifying priorities for further, more concentrated research to focus on. Broadly, we categorize these in terms of identifying factors impacting wild animal welfare, developing tools for assessing wild animal welfare at scale (necessary for monitoring & evaluating interventions), and scoping wild animal welfare interventions. I summarize some highlights from each category here, and you can see the broad sweep of WAI’s external grantmaking allocation in Figure 1 below.

Measuring wild animal welfare

  • Does DNA methylation reflect environmental and social adversity?: This project is taking advantage of detailed biographical information assembled over decades of monitoring a single Rocky Mountains marmot population to test whether DNA methylation (a proxy for biological ageing) correlates with an index of early life adversity. This builds on previous work from this team, developing the index, and connects to the importance of juvenile welfare.
  • Harnessing machine learning for the non-invasive assessment of wild fish welfare: This project builds on a previous WAI-funded project that developed a judgement bias test for juvenile wild fish by combining a similar approach with machine learning to make it more scalable. We hope that scalable wild animal welfare data collection will eventually lead to a ‘passive’ uptake of wild animal welfare into policy decisions (in addition to the effects of active advocacy) simply by making such data available to decision makers. For example, if someone is performing an environmental impact assessment, they will come across evidence of welfare impacts in their  literature searches alongside evidence of population/conservation impacts.
  • Feeling salty: A welfare framework for estuarine fishes: This project aims to identify a specific set of indicators that are both informative and feasible for monitoring the welfare of fish in estuaries. We like that this project is explicitly about making WAWS practicable on the ground and integrating it into environmental impact assessments affecting large numbers of individuals. It’s the kind of project we’ll need to see repeated in many more ecological contexts.
  • Environmental drivers of welfare in urban rats: A multimodal field study of micro-habitat conditions and affective behavior: This project, hosted by Basis.ai, will develop a scalable monitoring platform for rat welfare using indicators validated in captivity. With one of the most promising near-term wild animal welfare interventions being rodent fertility control, this is just the kind of thing we’ll need to be able to monitor and optimize our interventions.
  • Developing an automated cognitive bias task for wild squirrels: This project will transfer a challenging but widely accepted method of welfare assessment in captivity to a wild rodent in a way that emphasizes scalability and cost-effectiveness.
  • Thermal imaging as a non-invasive welfare assessment tool for tracking the impact of environmental stressors across wild animal populations: This project seeks to validate eye temperature as a welfare indicator for wild birds. By using thermal cameras at feeding stations, the method should also be scalable and ideal for monitoring the impact of interventions based around fixed locations, like supplemental feeding or contraceptive bait stations.
  • Developing an approach for assessing the welfare of wild birds through the use of bioacoustics analysis and Assessing animal welfare from bioacoustic monitoring in red-billed choughs: These two similar projects, funded at the same time, are both developing passive acoustic monitoring to study wild bird welfare. This approach could also be automated and scaled at relatively low cost, and used alongside similar approaches, like thermal imaging.
  • Remote welfare assessment in wildlife using stand-off Raman spectroscopy: This project seeks to develop a method for measuring cortisol levels in the hair of wild mammals remotely, using Raman spectroscopy. Although cortisol is not the strongest welfare indicator by itself, the prospect of measuring it without even touching an animal provides great potential for large-scale automated welfare monitoring in combination with things like camera traps, thermal imaging and bioacoustics.
  • Developing, testing and validating indicators of wild insect welfare: This project will attempt to validate a suite of field-accessible welfare indicators for three common yet disparate insect species. Meghan Barrett of the Insect Welfare Research Society is also a collaborator.

Understanding factors affecting welfare

  • Stranding: a blessing or a curse? Testing assumptions of fish welfare during habitat fragmentation: This project is investigating what happens to welfare when drought separates fish populations into isolated and shrinking lakes. It is also a fellowship for a mission-aligned PhD student.
  • Evaluating wild animal welfare in landscapes of fear at urban-wildland interfaces: This project is investigating potential welfare impact of lizards’ fear response to suburban dangers, such as vehicles and cats. It is also a fellowship for a mission-aligned postdoc, and is investigating DNA methylation as a potential welfare indicator.
  • Parasites in the city: How is the impact of parasites on wild animal welfare affected by urbanization?: This project will evaluate the welfare impact of parasitic infections on grey squirrels and relate it to their age and other demographic factors in a QALY-like framework (‘welfare expectancy’).

Welfare interventions

  • Towards welfare-centered prescribed fire: With climate change increasing wildfire risk globally, there is increasing emphasis on forestry tactics such as controlled burns. This project will study how bush rats react to controlled burns and use that information to create welfare-focused guidelines that minimize impacts on wild rodent welfare. These guidelines could also help reduce the wild animal suffering caused by unplanned/naturogenic wildfires.

  • Does diet mediate effects of sublethal parasitic infections on host welfare?: This project is primarily studying the impact of intestinal nematode parasites on wild mouse welfare and how that effect interacts with other risk factors. However, because it takes an experimental approach by deworming some of the mice in expectation of seeing a positive welfare impact, it could also be considered a trial of a wild animal welfare intervention.

     

Figure 1: How WAI’s grantmaking has broken out across taxa (note that rodents are distinguished as a priority group from non-rodent mammals), project types, and welfare factor categories since our 2023 calls for proposals (which is when our metrics became more consistent). It reflects the consequences of some meaningful prioritization decisions on our part: 1) lots of funding to rodent projects; 2) significant funding to invertebrate projects and almost all of it to projects whose primary purpose is "measuring welfare" (because that remains the primary barrier to understanding and improving invertebrate welfare, even more than with other taxa); 3) generally diversified funding across taxa and welfare factors. These reflect our strategy of building and maintaining a broad field that is working towards a better world for all animals, while nudging its priorities towards the most numerous animals and the most important and tractable causes of suffering. Note that for projects that considered welfare factors from multiple categories, the budget was divided equally across those categories.

 

What we haven’t seen enough of

We are happy with the foundation of wild animal welfare research we’ve seeded over the past few years, and excited to see those projects’ results. However, as I alluded to earlier, most of our early grantmaking took a big-tent, experimental approach, emphasizing giving a shot to scientists who were new to the field (which was almost everyone at the beginning) and initiating projects on diverse species using diverse methods. There is necessarily a trade-off, and that brings me to the topic of what we haven’t optimized for up to this point but need to see more of going forward. We haven’t seen enough projects building on each other. I mentioned one standout example above, which is the project using machine learning to evaluate attention bias in wild fish. However, this is one of a handful of exceptions.

The long timescale of academic research is probably a huge factor. From the point when we fund a project, it usually takes months to start; sometimes because the principal investigator must recruit a PhD student or postdoc, or permits must be obtained. Then, the pace of many projects is limited by field seasons. Once the data is collected, the pace of analysis and writing is largely in the hands of the researchers, but it is challenging, often requiring coordination of a whole team of researchers who may have other projects or teaching responsibilities. Then, there’s the academic publishing process, which is genuinely inefficient (to put it mildly). The net result of this is that most of the projects WAI has funded have not published their results yet, and the ones that have are mostly from the earliest funding rounds, when we funded projects on the widest variety of themes and methods. Funding wide early was a strategic choice, since our first priority was introducing new people to the field and demonstrating its scope and relevance across many disciplines. However, all this means that there has been little opportunity for new grant applicants to build on or even learn about previous WAI-funded research unless they already collaborate with the relevant grantees. Moreover, each year we’ve received a larger share of projects focusing on abundant/neglected taxa and more important causes of suffering, and we’ve generally prioritized those over continuing to fund less impactful research directions. We’re really pleased to be seeing that shift and think we’ve taken the right approach so far, but we are approaching a pivot point. Ultimately, it is crucial for projects to build on each other and develop into deep research programs because actually improving wild animal welfare is such a complex, multi-step challenge.

  

The next phase of WAI’s strategy

If our initial priority of establishing mainstream acceptance of WAWS was phase 1 of WAI’s strategy (~2019-2023), and phase 2 involved emphasizing the distinctiveness of the field by leaning more into our priority themes while still focusing on growing the field (~2023-26), we are now entering a third phase. To accelerate progress improving wild animal welfare by building on this initial foundation of research initiatives, and to encourage long-term commitment to WAWS by reinvesting in the researchers who have demonstrated enthusiasm and aptitude for WAWS, the next phase of WAI’s strategy will emphasize the development of research programs over individual projects, and developing institutions through networks of researchers.

We have lots of plans and changes in store to address those objectives. I won’t share anything here that we aren’t prepared to share with the scientists in our network, but I can describe some of the most important changes that will be coming to our grants program when our next call for proposals launches this fall. Currently, we offer three main types of research grants that are primarily distinguished by their budget limits and competitiveness. We are now introducing all-new grant types, with much more specific purposes. These grant types will be offered simultaneously, but are designed to lead from one type to the next for any given research program or study system:

  • The first stage will be a Seed Grant (<$30k), which are for observational or pilot studies intended to identify candidate welfare indicators that could be subjected to a more rigorous validation experiment. For example, I have rescued dozens of injured garden snails, and I’ve noticed a few things that might be relevant to welfare: the posture and rigidity of their eye stalks seems to vary depending on the circumstances, and how much they retract their body into their shells when they sleep seems to vary among individuals. Those hypotheses aren’t developed or grounded enough to warrant a validation experiment, but with a Seed Grant I could quantify those snail behaviors alongside welfare-relevant conditions (such as competition or parasite load) to look for statistical associations as a first step. (Incidentally, we recently funded a welfare indicator validation project for snails!)
  • For better-understood taxa and contexts, a Seed Grant may not be necessary and a researcher can proceed directly to the first major grant type, a Validation Grant (<$200k). These projects will be entirely focused on testing the validity of potential welfare indicators through a structured process originally proposed by Heather Browning and applied by WAI’s Research Manager Michaël Beaulieu and others (e.g. Beaulieu 2024). The validation process is absolutely essential for truly understanding wild animal welfare because it confirms that we are actually assessing welfare. However, it is highly rigorous, and we’ve found that many grant applicants understandably want to skip ahead to the more interesting and motivating questions. That’s why we’re introducing a specific grant type dedicated to this kind of project.
  • We are also tightening our requirements for projects’ welfare assessment frameworks, which will give grantees who successfully deliver on a validation project a distinct advantage if they subsequently propose to address those more interesting questions via the next grant type, a Welfare Ecology Grant (<$200k). These grants will focus on assessing how wild animal welfare is affected by ecological factors, such as resource availability, disease, etc., within particular ecosystems. The objective of these grants is to gradually build up a picture of the causal network of factors so that interventions or policies can eventually be devised to improve wild animal welfare.
  • Intervention Grants will support that final step, and will debut next year, with our 2027 call for proposals. These projects will run field trials of interventions based on justified hypotheses and monitoring and evaluation tools of the sort developed through Validation Grants and Welfare Ecology Grants. Currently, we do not have these pieces in place for any wild animal welfare intervention, although we have funded projects working towards a foundation for testing a few potential interventions, including rodent fertility control and bird feeding. Between now and the launch of Intervention Grants, WAI’s research team will also be developing a new internal research agenda for 2027-29 by working backwards from potential wild animal welfare interventions to identify recurring research questions that would need to be answered in order to recommend for or against multiple specific interventions. Our internal research agenda will focus on broad conceptual or methodological questions that emerge, but other lessons from this process will inform what we ask of future Intervention Grant applicants.

 

Figure 2: The progression path through WAI grant types. A grant applicant seeking to break ground on a new research program would first apply for a Seed Grant if their focal species and the welfare challenges they face are poorly understood. If the basic biology of the species is reasonably well understood, but it has not been studied in welfare terms in the wild, they may apply directly for a Validation Grant. If the applicant is already an experienced wild animal welfare scientist (based on publication record) and there are validated indicators for the proposed focal species (or close relatives), they may apply directly for a Welfare Ecology Grant. We expect that it will take multiple Welfare Ecology Grant projects (by the same or different teams) for most research programs to mature to the point where they can proceed to an Intervention Grant.

 

We will also be experimenting with ways to hasten the handover of new knowledge between projects, such as requiring grantees to commit to a timeline for publication (or at least pre-print sharing) and facilitating more small-scale meet-ups for researchers working on related problems (like this one organized by WAI grantees working on applying cognitive bias tests to wild animals). Investing in WAWS institutions, particularly research centers, could also help accelerate research feedback loops, since co-located wild animal welfare scientists should be relatively up-to-date with each other’s findings.

Conclusion

WAI’s first 7 years of field-building for wild animal welfare science has laid the foundations of a recognized and growing field (albeit one still almost fully dependent on WAI for funding). We have prioritized establishing awareness and legitimacy for the field, publishing research that articulates key concepts of the field, and awarding research grants that showcase the scope and priorities of the field while giving scientists from adjacent fields an opportunity to incorporate wild animal welfare into their personal research programs. A trade-off of this approach is that research has been less concentrated towards any single breakthrough or intervention. However, we are already seeing this pay off in terms of a broad base of interest and support for wild animal welfare science. Our grants have seeded many compelling avenues for further development, and we think the field has reached a stage where WAI-funded research effort can become more consolidated into projects that build on one another. This is a tactical evolution to help ensure the coordination-related benefits of an academic field are actually realized in terms of research towards the most pressing and action-relevant questions.

However, as I alluded to earlier, most of our early grantmaking took a big-tent, experimental approach, emphasizing giving a shot to scientists who were new to the field (which was almost everyone at the beginning) and initiating projects on diverse species using diverse methods. There is necessarily a trade-off, and that brings me to the topic of what we haven’t optimized for up to this point but need to see more of going forward. We haven’t seen enough projects building on each other. I mentioned one standout example above, which is the project using machine learning to evaluate attention bias in wild fish. However, this is one of a handful of exceptions.

The long timescale of academic research is probably a huge factor. From the point when we fund a project, it usually takes months to start; sometimes because the principal investigator must recruit a PhD student or postdoc, or permits must be obtained. Then, the pace of many projects is limited by field seasons. Once the data is collected, the pace of analysis and writing is largely in the hands of the researchers, but it is challenging, often requiring coordination of a whole team of researchers who may have other projects or teaching responsibilities. Then, there’s the academic publishing process, which is genuinely inefficient (to put it mildly). The net result of this is that most of the projects WAI has funded have not published their results yet, and the ones that have are mostly from the earliest funding rounds, when we funded projects on the widest variety of themes and methods. Funding wide early was a strategic choice, since our first priority was introducing new people to the field and demonstrating its scope and relevance across many disciplines. However, all this means that there has been little opportunity for new grant applicants to build on or even learn about previous WAI-funded research unless they already collaborate with the relevant grantees. Moreover, each year we’ve received a larger share of projects focusing on abundant/neglected taxa and more important causes of suffering, and we’ve generally prioritized those over continuing to fund less impactful research directions. We’re really pleased to be seeing that shift and think we’ve taken the right approach so far, but we are approaching a pivot point. Ultimately, it is crucial for projects to build on each other and develop into deep research programs because actually improving wild animal welfare is such a complex, multi-step challenge.

  

The next phase of WAI’s strategy

If our initial priority of establishing mainstream acceptance of WAWS was phase 1 of WAI’s strategy (~2019-2023), and phase 2 involved emphasizing the distinctiveness of the field by leaning more into our priority themes while still focusing on growing the field (~2023-26), we are now entering a third phase. To accelerate progress improving wild animal welfare by building on this initial foundation of research initiatives, and to encourage long-term commitment to WAWS by reinvesting in the researchers who have demonstrated enthusiasm and aptitude for WAWS, the next phase of WAI’s strategy will emphasize the development of research programs over individual projects, and developing institutions through networks of researchers.

We have lots of plans and changes in store to address those objectives. I won’t share anything here that we aren’t prepared to share with the scientists in our network, but I can describe some of the most important changes that will be coming to our grants program when our next call for proposals launches this fall. Currently, we offer three main types of research grants that are primarily distinguished by their budget limits and competitiveness. We are now introducing all-new grant types, with much more specific purposes. These grant types will be offered simultaneously, but are designed to lead from one type to the next for any given research program or study system:

  • The first stage will be a Seed Grant (<$30k), which are for observational or pilot studies intended to identify candidate welfare indicators that could be subjected to a more rigorous validation experiment. For example, I have rescued dozens of injured garden snails, and I’ve noticed a few things that might be relevant to welfare: the posture and rigidity of their eye stalks seems to vary depending on the circumstances, and how much they retract their body into their shells when they sleep seems to vary among individuals. Those hypotheses aren’t developed or grounded enough to warrant a validation experiment, but with a Seed Grant I could quantify those snail behaviors alongside welfare-relevant conditions (such as competition or parasite load) to look for statistical associations as a first step. (Incidentally, we recently funded a welfare indicator validation project for snails!)
  • For better-understood taxa and contexts, a Seed Grant may not be necessary and a researcher can proceed directly to the first major grant type, a Validation Grant (<$200k). These projects will be entirely focused on testing the validity of potential welfare indicators through a structured process originally proposed by Heather Browning and applied by WAI’s Research Manager Michaël Beaulieu and others (e.g. Beaulieu 2024). The validation process is absolutely essential for truly understanding wild animal welfare because it confirms that we are actually assessing welfare. However, it is highly rigorous, and we’ve found that many grant applicants understandably want to skip ahead to the more interesting and motivating questions. That’s why we’re introducing a specific grant type dedicated to this kind of project.
  • We are also tightening our requirements for projects’ welfare assessment frameworks, which will give grantees who successfully deliver on a validation project a distinct advantage if they subsequently propose to address those more interesting questions via the next grant type, a Welfare Ecology Grant (<$200k). These grants will focus on assessing how wild animal welfare is affected by ecological factors, such as resource availability, disease, etc., within particular ecosystems. The objective of these grants is to gradually build up a picture of the causal network of factors so that interventions or policies can eventually be devised to improve wild animal welfare.
  • Intervention Grants will support that final step, and will debut next year, with our 2027 call for proposals. These projects will run field trials of interventions based on justified hypotheses and monitoring and evaluation tools of the sort developed through Validation Grants and Welfare Ecology Grants. Currently, we do not have these pieces in place for any wild animal welfare intervention, although we have funded projects working towards a foundation for testing a few potential interventions, including rodent fertility control and bird feeding. Between now and the launch of Intervention Grants, WAI’s research team will also be developing a new internal research agenda for 2027-29 by working backwards from potential wild animal welfare interventions to identify recurring research questions that would need to be answered in order to recommend for or against multiple specific interventions. Our internal research agenda will focus on broad conceptual or methodological questions that emerge, but other lessons from this process will inform what we ask of future Intervention Grant applicants.

 

Figure 2: The progression path through WAI grant types. A grant applicant seeking to break ground on a new research program would first apply for a Seed Grant if their focal species and the welfare challenges they face are poorly understood. If the basic biology of the species is reasonably well understood, but it has not been studied in welfare terms in the wild, they may apply directly for a Validation Grant. If the applicant is already an experienced wild animal welfare scientist (based on publication record) and there are validated indicators for the proposed focal species (or close relatives), they may apply directly for a Welfare Ecology Grant. We expect that it will take multiple Welfare Ecology Grant projects (by the same or different teams) for most research programs to mature to the point where they can proceed to an Intervention Grant.

 

We will also be experimenting with ways to hasten the handover of new knowledge between projects, such as requiring grantees to commit to a timeline for publication (or at least pre-print sharing) and facilitating more small-scale meet-ups for researchers working on related problems (like this one organized by WAI grantees working on applying cognitive bias tests to wild animals). Investing in WAWS institutions, particularly research centers, could also help accelerate research feedback loops, since co-located wild animal welfare scientists should be relatively up-to-date with each other’s findings.

Conclusion

WAI’s first 7 years of field-building for wild animal welfare science has laid the foundations of a recognized and growing field (albeit one still almost fully dependent on WAI for funding). We have prioritized establishing awareness and legitimacy for the field, publishing research that articulates key concepts of the field, and awarding research grants that showcase the scope and priorities of the field while giving scientists from adjacent fields an opportunity to incorporate wild animal welfare into their personal research programs. A trade-off of this approach is that research has been less concentrated towards any single breakthrough or intervention. However, we are already seeing this pay off in terms of a broad base of interest and support for wild animal welfare science. Our grants have seeded many compelling avenues for further development, and we think the field has reached a stage where WAI-funded research effort can become more consolidated into projects that build on one another. This is a tactical evolution to help ensure the coordination-related benefits of an academic field are actually realized in terms of research towards the most pressing and action-relevant questions.

item.description:
Published on August 19, 2026 2:28 PM GMT

Sentient Futures Summit (SFS) Bay Area 2027 is a three-day conference taking place on March 12-14, 2027 @ Mox, San Francisco, exploring the impact of AI and other emerging technologies on sentient non-humans, both biological and potentially artificial. This is the 7th conference of our series, which has served as a premier meeting place for those working to ensure that non-human sentient beings are not left behind in the long-term future.

What to expect:

  1. A range of talks, workshops, and discussions across animal welfare, AI safety, philosophy of mind, and AI welfare
  2. Opportunities to network with potential collaborators and funders in a focused and intimate setting
  3. Deep, interdisciplinary conversations on future-oriented solutions that reduce non-human suffering

📣 The Call for Speakers is Now Open!

We’re looking for a range of submissions spanning ethical considerations in AI systems, animal welfare in the age of transformative AI, philosophy of mind and machine consciousness, as well as AI governance and policy. We’re accepting applications from speakers (long-form and lightning talks) and facilitators (workshops and other interactive formats).  

If you have a compelling idea that pushes the conversation on non-human welfare forward, we'd love to hear it. Speakers and facilitators receive complimentary tickets. Submit your application by October 16 here.

Already on our list of tentative attendees, we have:

  1. Michael Andregg, Founder/CEO @ Eon Systems

item.title: Hiring Good In-House Counsel - a braindump
item.description:
Published on August 18, 2026 6:52 PM GMT

I'm Molly Kovite, General Counsel at Coefficient Giving. I joined in 2021 as the organization's first lawyer and have since grown the team to (soon to be) seven lawyers and three legal admins.

Over the past couple of months, a number of AI safety organizations have asked me about whether they should hire in-house counsel and if so, what they should look for. This post is my attempt to write down what I've told them: how to tell when you've outgrown outside counsel, what in-house counsel does and doesn't get you, how to scope the role, and how to run a process that actually tells you whether someone will be good at it. This is one lawyer's experience at one organization, so treat it as calibrated opinion rather than settled wisdom. I'd be glad to hear where people disagree.

How do I know when I should hire an in-house attorney?

Some signs to look for:

  • You’re unsure whether you’re bringing the right things to outside counsel
  • Important plans or projects have been derailed or significantly delayed two or more times in ~6 months due to unexpected legal issues cropping up, despite running things by outside counsel
  • You feel uncertain about the quality and calibration of the advice outside counsel is giving you, and this is true of more than just one or two external lawyers
  • People at your org are having to spend an annoying amount of their time talking to outside counsel

One of the real values of in-house counsel is issue spotting, which is something that outside counsel can't really do because they're not broadly aware of what you're doing. They're only aware of what you bring to them, so the first indication that you might want to consider in-house counsel is that you feel pretty unsure whether you’re bringing the right things to outside counsel.

Another big value add of in-house counsel is that they can learn your culture and calibrate their legal advice to your organization's priorities, risk tolerance, and communication style. Even if you work with excellent outside counsel, they're just not gonna be able to do this as well. While in-house counsel won't have the breadth of knowledge of an entire law firm's worth of attorneys, when working with outside counsel, they'll be able to present the issue to outside counsel much more succinctly than a non-lawyer in-house. They'll be able to keep the outside counsel focused on the specific issue, which can be more of a challenge than you'd expect.

They'll be able to push back when outside counsel is being overly conservative, which they tend to be, and they'll be able to drill into what the actual legal and enforcement issues are more confidently than a non-lawyer in the same conversation. They'll be able to communicate that advice back to the rest of the team because they'll understand the level of knowledge and context that the rest of their team members have.

So if you find yourself frustrated with working with outside counsel because you feel they're too conservative, you don't know how seriously to take their advice, and their communication style is not working for you, that's probably a good reason to consider at least fractional in-house counsel. Though it's also probably a good reason to consider changing outside counsel.

What are some of the downsides of hiring in-house counsel?

Attorneys do tend to be among the higher-paid employees at a given organization, so cost is definitely something to keep in mind. If your annual legal bills are in the $100,000 to $200,000 range, you're probably not going to consume a full attorney's worth of legal services.

You could consider hiring a fractional general counsel - an experienced lawyer who integrates into your organization but works on a part-time basis and may do so as a contractor across multiple organizations. You might be a bit less likely to get a really ideal culture fit or mission-motivated hire if you go this route.

Because whoever you hire will have limited expertise as compared to a whole law firm, you won't be able to just hire one lawyer and get those outside counsel costs down to zero unless what you're doing is incredibly specific (such that you can just hire one person with that skill set). Even if that's the case, lawyers don't like to operate alone, especially on high-stakes issues, so an in-house counsel would likely want to at least occasionally get a sanity check from outside counsel on important matters. And it’s arguable whether this is a feature or a bug, but having in-house counsel won’t even necessarily reduce your spend on outside counsel at all. They might come in and notice a bunch of compliance issues that need to be fixed, or notice things that the organization wasn’t previously getting advice on. So possibly more money and annoyance upfront buys you more resilience and less chaos down the line.

You could also consider hiring an attorney that also covers other operations portfolios; attorneys are often good operators who slot into other realms with relative ease. This is especially true of compliance-heavy realms like running a grants team, running a contracting team, or employment and HR functions.

This does create some issues on the margins about when legal privilege applies, although I think people are often too worried about maintaining privilege. Privilege only matters if you end up going to litigation, and most things are just not at risk of going to litigation. The privilege issue of having an attorney working on non-attorney matters is that if an attorney is acting in e.g. their capacity as an HR advisor, then a given conversation would not be privileged, because the attorney is not giving legal advice, but HR advice. Whereas if they're acting in their capacity as an attorney, then a conversation would be privileged, and sometimes there's going to be ambiguity about that.

How do I scope the role?

You probably won't successfully predict exactly what the role will look like if you've never had in-house counsel before, and that's okay. When I was hired at Coefficient Giving (Open Philanthropy at the time) the basic idea was that I could help the org save money on some of the more rote stuff, like updating our grant agreement templates and reviewing contracts and that kind of thing.

It became apparent pretty quickly that I could add more value in other ways, especially since I was way more attuned to our organization’s goals and risk tolerance than outside counsel were. So my role changed a lot over time. I don't know whether that's more or less likely to happen with legal roles than other roles, but I think in general, as long as the needs of the organization are being met, having flexibility to take advantage of your employees' biggest value adds is a good thing.

That said, you do, of course, need some sense of what this person is going to do all day every day. If there is a person who is currently working with outside counsel, you should expect that that person will only rarely need to interact with outside counsel after in-house counsel has been hired. Not because in-house counsel will do all the work that outside counsel is doing, but because in-house counsel can be the one to interact with outside counsel. The work stream of interacting with outside counsel should be taken off everyone's plate.

That means in-house counsel will have to have some basic understanding of the work of anyone who interacts with outside counsel, so getting spun up on that knowledge will be a major component of their first several weeks. It's also likely that when in-house counsel first starts, they should do a basic audit of whatever compliance processes and systems are currently in place, as well as any portfolios that might carry some legal risk.

The basic portfolios that I would expect to exist at many/most organizations are:

  • Board matters and governance
  • HR and employment
  • Contract review (which would include grant agreements, where relevant)
  • Tax and regulatory compliance
  • Possibly some lobbying and political law
  • Maybe data privacy and document retention

What basic characteristics should I be looking for in an in-house counsel?

You want:

  • A good lawyer
    • Spots important issues
    • Draws correct conclusions from their legal research
    • When areas of law are unsettled, offers a range of interpretations that are well reasoned and defensible
    • Thinks in terms of tradeoffs and makes the available tradeoffs clear
    • Thinks creatively to generate solutions that minimize risk while achieving organizational goals
    • Has enough time practicing under their belt that they can do these things fluidly, without supervision (law school doesn’t make you ready to practice law)
  • Who communicates in a way that is native to your organization
  • Understands and internalizes the org’s mission well enough to make judgment calls the way the org would want when there's no time to ask
  • Knows when to be detail oriented and knows when to move forward quickly with less precision

You probably want other things too.

One thing that is somewhat unique to legal hiring is that mission alignment might matter a little bit less than for other roles. I think this because the legal profession is inherently somewhat mercenary. That’s not to say that there aren't tons of practicing lawyers who are doing what they're doing because they are motivated by a mission; but ultimately, as a lawyer, you have an ethical duty to zealously represent your client no matter who your client is. That is at the heart of the profession. Every lawyer has had experience advocating for something that they weren't 100% heart and soul bought into - and they can do it well because they believe that’s necessary to the functioning of the legal profession.

How should I design my work test(s)?

It’s pretty standard in our eco-system to conduct work tests as part of a hiring process. Historically that’s been pretty non-standard in the legal profession (though is probably normal in tech now), but I’ve received almost no negative feedback about that process. When I went through it myself I found that not only did it give me an opportunity to show I could do the job despite my lack of experience in the relevant fields of law, but also it gave me some insight into whether I would like the type of work I’d be doing. It’s a win across the board.

Designing and grading a good work test can be a bit tricky, especially as AI gets better and better at short and medium time-horizon tasks. Ideally, you just pull the work test from the real world and change a few facts and perhaps amalgamate two or three scenarios into one scenario so that there's a denser set of issues to work with. You’ll likely want to test for:

  • Risk calibration
  • Communication style
  • Ability to get familiar with an area of law and a set of facts relatively quickly
  • Willingness to flag uncertainty

One thing to look out for is that someone new to the area of law that your work touches on takes an incorrect turn very early in the chain of reasoning. It can be a totally reasonable misunderstanding, or even a reasonable interpretation of text that just happens to not be consistent with how the law has developed in practice. This can lead to the person getting to a pretty legally wrong but very reasonable outcome. I recommend being very forgiving in those circumstances.

One thing I found to be particularly helpful is to frame a test as a draft of a response to a client to be reviewed by a more senior lawyer on the team. So the test is both to draft the response to the client, but also to draft the email to the more senior lawyer flagging what parts they especially think need review. This framing makes it much more likely that the candidate will actually tag uncertainties, so you'll get a much more calibrated sense of: in real life, would this person have actually sent incorrect advice, or would they have consulted outside counsel or another expert on the right things such that their mistake would have been caught? It also gives you two different frames in which to evaluate the communication style. And lastly, the AIs, when I last did this (June of 2026), had a harder time doing well in the meta frame than they did with just a straightforward email-a-client test.

You'll also want to make sure your work test isn't just a dense series of legal issues, and instead is a broad scenario of "Hey, we want to do this thing. Here are some concerns." That's how issues get presented to lawyers, and often the client's concern is totally orthogonal to what the actual legal concerns should be. I don't like work tests that have red herrings, but I do think it's worth including legal issues aside from just the one that the prompt specifically draws attention to.

One thing that is particularly valuable to evaluate in legal writing is whether the lawyer has appropriately identified and summarized what they understand your goal to be at the beginning. That way, you can understand and make sure that you're on the same page about that. Have they created a document that allows you to skip through the reasoning and find the conclusions, and then go back and double-check the reasoning if you want to get into that level of detail? That kind of formatting ends up being of outsized importance in legal writing.

It's probably useful to have both a lawyer and a non-lawyer grade these work tests, and they don't necessarily have to reconcile their grades. The lawyer is going to respond more viscerally to incorrect legal conclusions and not notice when someone is drifting into slightly difficult-to-understand legalese. The non-lawyer is probably in a better position to evaluate communication style and also how informed they feel about risk calibration.

What should I look for in interviews?

This is probably idiosyncratic to your particular organization, but here are a couple of thoughts.

One theory I've had as I've built my team is that, by default, people don't really want to talk to lawyers. It's a bit like being sent to the principal's office. So to compensate for this, I've tried to build a team that is friendly and fun to interact with, in addition to being mission-oriented and excited about the work that our organization is doing. If your lawyer is someone that people like gossiping with, they're going to know more about what's happening at the organization, and that allows the lawyer to better protect the organization.

I don't think that's absolutely necessary to be successful in-house counsel. What people care about more than anything is getting good, calibrated legal advice and coming away feeling like the lawyer had their back, rather than feeling like the lawyer was trying to justify their icky feelings about what you're trying to do.

So aside from maybe considering whether this person is someone that colleagues would genuinely look forward to interacting with, just look for the things you traditionally look for in a lawyer. Do you feel confused about what they're saying? When you push back on something do they get flustered or double down, or do they pause and consider? Do they react as though risk is a moral rather than legal issue? Do they go on at length without allowing you an opportunity to interject or course correct?

If you’ve had experience with outside counsel, you’ll probably already have a feel for characteristics of lawyers you do and do not like working with. Think through those interactions and jot them down!

That means in-house counsel will have to have some basic understanding of the work of anyone who interacts with outside counsel, so getting spun up on that knowledge will be a major component of their first several weeks. It's also likely that when in-house counsel first starts, they should do a basic audit of whatever compliance processes and systems are currently in place, as well as any portfolios that might carry some legal risk.

The basic portfolios that I would expect to exist at many/most organizations are:

  • Board matters and governance
  • HR and employment
  • Contract review (which would include grant agreements, where relevant)
  • Tax and regulatory compliance
  • Possibly some lobbying and political law
  • Maybe data privacy and document retention

What basic characteristics should I be looking for in an in-house counsel?

You want:

  • A good lawyer
    • Spots important issues
    • Draws correct conclusions from their legal research
    • When areas of law are unsettled, offers a range of interpretations that are well reasoned and defensible
    • Thinks in terms of tradeoffs and makes the available tradeoffs clear
    • Thinks creatively to generate solutions that minimize risk while achieving organizational goals
    • Has enough time practicing under their belt that they can do these things fluidly, without supervision (law school doesn’t make you ready to practice law)
  • Who communicates in a way that is native to your organization
  • Understands and internalizes the org’s mission well enough to make judgment calls the way the org would want when there's no time to ask
  • Knows when to be detail oriented and knows when to move forward quickly with less precision

You probably want other things too.

One thing that is somewhat unique to legal hiring is that mission alignment might matter a little bit less than for other roles. I think this because the legal profession is inherently somewhat mercenary. That’s not to say that there aren't tons of practicing lawyers who are doing what they're doing because they are motivated by a mission; but ultimately, as a lawyer, you have an ethical duty to zealously represent your client no matter who your client is. That is at the heart of the profession. Every lawyer has had experience advocating for something that they weren't 100% heart and soul bought into - and they can do it well because they believe that’s necessary to the functioning of the legal profession.

How should I design my work test(s)?

It’s pretty standard in our eco-system to conduct work tests as part of a hiring process. Historically that’s been pretty non-standard in the legal profession (though is probably normal in tech now), but I’ve received almost no negative feedback about that process. When I went through it myself I found that not only did it give me an opportunity to show I could do the job despite my lack of experience in the relevant fields of law, but also it gave me some insight into whether I would like the type of work I’d be doing. It’s a win across the board.

Designing and grading a good work test can be a bit tricky, especially as AI gets better and better at short and medium time-horizon tasks. Ideally, you just pull the work test from the real world and change a few facts and perhaps amalgamate two or three scenarios into one scenario so that there's a denser set of issues to work with. You’ll likely want to test for:

  • Risk calibration
  • Communication style
  • Ability to get familiar with an area of law and a set of facts relatively quickly
  • Willingness to flag uncertainty

One thing to look out for is that someone new to the area of law that your work touches on takes an incorrect turn very early in the chain of reasoning. It can be a totally reasonable misunderstanding, or even a reasonable interpretation of text that just happens to not be consistent with how the law has developed in practice. This can lead to the person getting to a pretty legally wrong but very reasonable outcome. I recommend being very forgiving in those circumstances.

One thing I found to be particularly helpful is to frame a test as a draft of a response to a client to be reviewed by a more senior lawyer on the team. So the test is both to draft the response to the client, but also to draft the email to the more senior lawyer flagging what parts they especially think need review. This framing makes it much more likely that the candidate will actually tag uncertainties, so you'll get a much more calibrated sense of: in real life, would this person have actually sent incorrect advice, or would they have consulted outside counsel or another expert on the right things such that their mistake would have been caught? It also gives you two different frames in which to evaluate the communication style. And lastly, the AIs, when I last did this (June of 2026), had a harder time doing well in the meta frame than they did with just a straightforward email-a-client test.

You'll also want to make sure your work test isn't just a dense series of legal issues, and instead is a broad scenario of "Hey, we want to do this thing. Here are some concerns." That's how issues get presented to lawyers, and often the client's concern is totally orthogonal to what the actual legal concerns should be. I don't like work tests that have red herrings, but I do think it's worth including legal issues aside from just the one that the prompt specifically draws attention to.

One thing that is particularly valuable to evaluate in legal writing is whether the lawyer has appropriately identified and summarized what they understand your goal to be at the beginning. That way, you can understand and make sure that you're on the same page about that. Have they created a document that allows you to skip through the reasoning and find the conclusions, and then go back and double-check the reasoning if you want to get into that level of detail? That kind of formatting ends up being of outsized importance in legal writing.

It's probably useful to have both a lawyer and a non-lawyer grade these work tests, and they don't necessarily have to reconcile their grades. The lawyer is going to respond more viscerally to incorrect legal conclusions and not notice when someone is drifting into slightly difficult-to-understand legalese. The non-lawyer is probably in a better position to evaluate communication style and also how informed they feel about risk calibration.

What should I look for in interviews?

This is probably idiosyncratic to your particular organization, but here are a couple of thoughts.

One theory I've had as I've built my team is that, by default, people don't really want to talk to lawyers. It's a bit like being sent to the principal's office. So to compensate for this, I've tried to build a team that is friendly and fun to interact with, in addition to being mission-oriented and excited about the work that our organization is doing. If your lawyer is someone that people like gossiping with, they're going to know more about what's happening at the organization, and that allows the lawyer to better protect the organization.

I don't think that's absolutely necessary to be successful in-house counsel. What people care about more than anything is getting good, calibrated legal advice and coming away feeling like the lawyer had their back, rather than feeling like the lawyer was trying to justify their icky feelings about what you're trying to do.

So aside from maybe considering whether this person is someone that colleagues would genuinely look forward to interacting with, just look for the things you traditionally look for in a lawyer. Do you feel confused about what they're saying? When you push back on something do they get flustered or double down, or do they pause and consider? Do they react as though risk is a moral rather than legal issue? Do they go on at length without allowing you an opportunity to interject or course correct?

If you’ve had experience with outside counsel, you’ll probably already have a feel for characteristics of lawyers you do and do not like working with. Think through those interactions and jot them down!

item.title: Thoughts on Taking OpenAI Foundation Funding
item.description:
Published on August 20, 2026 1:00 PM GMT

In May 2025 I met Yo Shavit, who was working on national security policy at OpenAI and was thinking about how to prepare for a future in which models could seriously assist attackers in creating pandemics. We had a call, and when I shared notes with my team their main response was: "maybe start with not making models that can do that?"

Which is, in many ways, fair: by continuing to push the frontier in biological capabilities, OpenAI's actions were making things worse on many of the problems SecureBio is trying to solve. But OpenAI stopping wouldn't have resolved the problem: other firms were pushing quickly too, and the economic incentives strongly favored rapid capability advancement. Making the world more resilient to pandemics needed to be a high priority regardless, especially in light of models' increasing ability to help people with biology.

When I thought about what our initial conversations might turn into, however, my primary concerns were whether that might (a) compromise SecureBio's ability to independently assess and criticize OpenAI's work or (b) make the world less safe via reducing model developers' motivation to improve safeguards. I do think there's something to both of these, which I get into more below, but it seemed well worth it to talk with Yo about how we could work together.

I explained how we were building an early warning system to flag outbreaks, especially engineered ones that could otherwise spread widely before detection. I described how metagenomic sequencing lets you see what nucleic acid sequences (DNA and RNA) are present in a sample, without choosing in advance which sequences to look for, and how we were piloting this on wastewater and nasal swabs. Over the next few months we discussed opportunities to accelerate our work, he introduced us to OpenAI cofounder Wojciech Zaremba, and both Yo and Wojciech left OpenAI PBC (the for-profit) for the OpenAI Foundation (OAIF). We continued talking to them in these new roles, and these discussions, plus a lot of due diligence, led to the $17.2M OAIF grant which we announced today. I'm incredibly excited about this grant, which will allow us to expand our monitoring system, reduce our turnaround time substantially,[1] and generally reduce the risk that something could spread widely before detection.

Which brings me back to the two concerns I mentioned above. On (a), independence, SecureBio has two divisions, Detection and AI. This grant funds Detection, while the AI side of SecureBio evaluates models from many firms, including OpenAI. The grant does not give OpenAI or OAIF any formal control over what anyone at SecureBio can say publicly about any models. That was important to us, but it was also key to OAIF: Yo was very clear that they did not want to influence SecureBio AI's work, and wanted to review our policies to make sure they were sufficiently robust.

That said, we should pay attention to incentives. While it looks to me like OAIF is making its own decisions, the two organizations are closely linked in a way that goes beyond the shared "OpenAI" name: the OpenAI Foundation's endowment is a ~1/4 stake in OpenAI PBC, and they have almost identical boards. Might the AI side of SecureBio pull punches in criticizing the PBC to increase the chances that OAIF gives Detection more money in the future?

SecureBio has systemic controls to mitigate conflicts of interests, including separate leadership, budgets, and deliverables, and the AI team has written up public docs on their principles and conflict of interest policy. But I think the strongest evidence here is from April, when the AI team was looking at GPT 5.5. The grant was at what I would consider its most sensitive stage: we had been working on it for months with very positive signals, but we still didn't have an answer. This was public internally, and AI leadership was looped in, but there was never a question of this affecting what the AI team published, and in their assessment they documented a range of concerns. The biggest was that across several benchmarks the model would appear to refuse a dangerous question by deflecting, but actually it would go on to provide the requested information by giving a highly-transferable related solution. On these benchmarks the safeguards were illusory, and the AI team released their evaluation while the grant was pending.

This concern with incentives, however, is not new with this grant. When the AI side evaluates a company's models, that company typically pays for the evaluation. For example, OpenAI PBC covered SecureBio's costs for the GPT 5.5 evaluation above. This is common with AI evals, and it's a tighter connection than this grant because there's no AI-Detection division insulating evaluators from financial incentives.

Still, this is a place where it takes continued effort to uphold standards, and if there's any indication that funding for Detection is being used as a lever to pressure our AI team on evals, I'll say so publicly and use whatever leverage I have to stop it (up to and including resignation). But I'm not expecting this, and I think the real worry is a subtle drift towards being more generous without anyone explicitly asking for anything. This is also a concern with funding from Anthropic employees, since SecureBio also evaluates Anthropic's work (ex). So if you see SecureBio put out anything unfairly positive towards OpenAI or Anthropic, or unfairly negative in overcorrecting for these incentives, please say so.

On (b), the question is whether this will let model developers take more risk. If we help them sleep better at night, knowing defenses are stronger, will they just push ahead faster during the day? I want us to be a complement to the frontier firms' internal safeguards, but what if we become a substitute?

A world sufficiently robust against catastrophic biorisk, where it doesn't matter what models are willing to explain because real-world protections are a full substitute for model safeguards, would be a fantastic place to be. We and many other projects are working towards that world! But there's a ton of work to get there. The worry is that AI firms perceive risk as lower and ease up on their safeguards when the risk is still unacceptably high.

I think this is directionally real, but as a direct substitute it's small compared to the reputational, legal (liability + risk of directives), and moral forces pushing firms to invest in safeguards. This grant will allow us to flag attacks earlier, but doesn't come close to mitigating the full impact of an attack and only covers one of several paths to large-scale biological harm. The first-order positive effects of making the world more robust to catastrophic biorisk are really very likely to outweigh the second-order effects of reducing safeguards; if I thought the other way around it would suggest that I should instead do or fund work (virus hunting?) that visibly increases risk in order to motivate others to step up, which seems like a terrible idea.

Separately but relatedly, there's also a "political cover" angle, where the PBC might point at this grant (even though it was made by OAIF) to say that they're doing something, taking off some external pressure. To the extent that this reduction in pressure lets them avoid costly actions that would do more to reduce risk, this is a loss, and it's my largest concern with this grant. Philanthropic funding should not be a license to act recklessly, and if they offer it as an excuse we shouldn't accept it. Please keep the pressure on OpenAI, and all the other frontier firms, to slow down and prioritize reducing the risk that their work leads to catastrophe. Even more important than pressuring firms, however, is advocacy for thoughtful AI regulation: this is a coordination problem where it's not in any individual firm's interest to slow down even though it is in humanity's interest collectively.

On balance I think this grant is strongly positive, and I'm much more worried that we won't do the best possible job pushing this work forward than that our efforts will let OpenAI and others ease up on their own work.

item.title: Effective Altruism and End-Times Fascism
item.description:
Published on August 19, 2026 9:58 PM GMT

I just read an article from The Guardian, written in April 2025 (I'm a bit behind on my reading ...). It's a good read, but that's noy why I share it here. What I want to highlight is something I'm seeing more and more, which is very negative portrayals and stereotyping of EA. 

Some EA's seem ok with this, or accept that it goes with the territory. I vehemently disagree. I would argue that bringing EA thinking to the centre of the Overton window would be the single most impactful achievement of the 21st century, and that it is something we need to take very seriously, and dedicate resources to.

 The rise of end times fascism | Far right (US) | The Guardian

This particular article is about the evil and danger of the fascist right-wing that is sweeping across the US and much of Europe. About a world in which empathy is seen as a great weakness, a world in which those opposing a climate armageddon are equated with Satan, a world of self-styled "Christian nationalism," where foreigners are enemies whom we torture to inspire the loyalty of the masses, ... well, you know, the world many of out elected leaders seem to inhabit. 

Then, while reading and sadly nodding my head in agreement with so much of the article, I came upon this text:

 "There is also effective altruism and longtermism, both of which skip over redistributive approaches to helping those in need in the here and now in favor of a cost-benefit approach to doing the most good in the long term. Though they can appear benign at first glance, these ideas are shot through with dangerous racial, ableist and gender biases about which parts of humanity are worth enhancing and saving – and which could be sacrificed for the supposed good of the whole. They also share a marked lack of interest in urgently addressing the underlying drivers of collapse – a responsible and rational goal that a growing cohort of figures now actively shun."

Those EA's who live in EA-bubbles probably do not realise just how badly EA is perceived in mainstream media. But this is The Guardian, a very liberal UK newspaper, and the article was written by two very well known liberal activists, Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. On almost any political or social question, The Guardian might be the world newspaper most aligned with EA's positions. But even there, this criminally false stereotyping of EA passes. If we were Donald Trump, we would sue for $10 billion for reputational damage, but we'd actually win.

And this is far from a one-off. Just this week, The Economist, another quite liberal outlet, published an article (paywalled) in which EA thinking was described as just "weird" and ideas like direct giving were ironically described as "exotic." And, of course, as usual, the first actual EA person named, the typical EA whose goal is to live a life of luxury but assuage their conscience through public displays of charity, was SBF. That is literally how many people see EA's.

 

Why does this matter?

Effective Altruism is a rare philosophy with the explicit goal of helping people and animals without any strings attached. You don't have to believe in bizarre metaphysical theories (but it's ok if you do). Everybody is welcome. You just need to want to help people and animals as much as you can. 

I don't need to convince this audience that EA is great...

The world would be so much better if everyone were exposed to this thinking in a positive way. But too many people either never hear of it at all, or hear about it as some weird nerdish cult. If you were to ask Americans which public figures might be EA's, they would probably name some of the most evil but clever humans who have ever lived, like Peter Thiel or Elon Musk. That's how EA is perceived, and that's why it's so hard to spread our message.

We need people to start thinking of typical EA's as more like Peter Singer or Rutger Bregman, who openly focus on helping and caring. Ir we could move the image of a typical EA closer to someone like Mr. Rogers or even Keanu Reeves, that would help balance things a bit and show the caring side that is often overlooked. 

Maybe we could even get some very popular people who are widely respected as decent people (George Clooney, Taylor Swift, Bruce Springsteen, Barack Obama, even Bono ...) to start speaking about EA in a positive way. 

It's easy to ignore this - we work away in our dark corner, not looking for respect or admiration, just doing what is right and helping people. We get to feel like martyrs, which is nice. But unfortunately, if we remain a tiny minority, we will always have limited impact, while those who know how to do PR (often the populists) will continue to move the world in the wrong direction.

IMHO, people across the rich world are struggling to find a philosophy that contradicts the horrific ideas they hear from Trump, Farage, Meloni, Vox, AfD, Orban, ... and they are struggling because so many politicians and parties (all the EPP aligned parties across the EU, the Democrats in the US) that should be providing that alternative have also moved far to the right and accepted many of the neofascist ideas so deeply that they are now considered moderate. 

EA has the potential to offer a clear view which matches with the true worldview of many people, including not just liberals but decent conservatives and true Christians. We don't have to be a political party, we just need to get the ideas out there, being discussed and given a fair hearing, rather than being dismissed as they are today. 

If we can get people asking themselves seriously if they would like to live in a world governed by EA thinking, I believe many would, because at heart people are good - we just need to give them the chance to show their true nature.
